note: Sections are placed at natural topic breaks found in Whisper transcripts of the archive.org files. start is in seconds; a section ends where the next begins.

1.title: The Ship of the Imagination
1.desc: "We're made of star stuff." Sagan sets out from the edge of the known universe, past colliding galaxies, quasars and Andromeda, to our own Milky Way, pulsars and all.
questions: Sagan says we're "a way for the cosmos to know itself." What does that mean to you, and does it change how you think about your own life?
He promises to be bold in speculation but careful to separate it from fact. Where in your own life do you blur the two?
Seeing Earth as one tiny planet among billions: does that make human life feel smaller or more precious? Why?

1.title: Stellar nurseries, then the long fall home
1.desc: An alien world reshaped by its inhabitants, the Orion Nebula where stars are born, then inward past Saturn, Jupiter and Mars to a blue world, third from the sun.
questions: Sagan imagines an alien world that its inhabitants have completely re-engineered. What would an outside observer conclude about us from how we've reshaped Earth?
Stars are born and die in the same galaxy at the same time. What other systems (cities, families, ideas) work that way?
Why do you think Sagan ends this long journey by coming home rather than going further out?

1.title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth with a stick
1.desc: Sticks, shadows and a well at Syene: a librarian in 3rd-century BC Egypt works out the size of the planet to within a few percent. Plus the Phoenicians who sailed around Africa.
questions: Eratosthenes measured the planet with sticks, shadows and a hired walker. What everyday observation have you ignored that might be hiding something big?
Someone else might have dismissed the report from Syene as an error. When is it right to trust an odd report, and when is it right to doubt it?
What would it take for you to actually test an idea yourself instead of taking someone's word for it?

1.title: The Library of Alexandria
1.desc: A walk through a reconstruction of the ancient world's greatest library: Euclid, Hipparchus, Hypatia, and the lost book of Aristarchus. What we lost, and how its rediscovery lit the Renaissance.
questions: The Library held nearly everything known, and still fell. What made it vulnerable, and is anything like that true of our knowledge today?
Ptolemy was brilliant and still "dead wrong" for 1,500 years. How do you tell the difference between being smart and being right?
If you could rescue one lost book from history, which would you pick and why?

1.title: The Cosmic Calendar
1.desc: All 15 billion years squeezed into one year. Every king, war and invention in the history books fits into the last ten seconds of December 31st.
questions: All of recorded history fits in the last few seconds of the Cosmic Calendar. How does that perspective change what you worry about?
Sagan says what happens in the first second of the next cosmic year depends on us. What do you think that first second looks like?
Does being so recent make humanity feel insignificant to you, or lucky?

2.title: The Heike crab: a samurai face shaped by fishermen
2.desc: A 12th-century sea battle, a drowned child emperor, and crabs whose shells bear a warrior's scowl. A perfect, eerie lesson in artificial selection.
questions: Fishermen shaped the Heike crab without ever meaning to. What are we selecting for today without realizing it (in animals, technology, or ourselves)?
Why is a story like this one more convincing than a textbook definition of selection?
Which domesticated plant or animal in your life would surprise you most if you saw its wild ancestor?

2.title: Natural selection and the first molecules of life
2.desc: Trilobites, Darwin and Wallace, the watchmaker argument, then the cosmic calendar of life: the organic soup, the first self-copying molecule, and DNA.
questions: The watchmaker argument felt obvious to people for centuries. Why do you think design is such an intuitive explanation?
"The secrets of evolution are time and death." How do you feel about death being part of what made us possible?
What's the most convincing piece of evidence for evolution to you, and why that one?

2.title: Four billion years in forty seconds
2.desc: From a soap-bubble cell to fish, amphibians, dinosaurs, shrews and us, ending in the famous morphing march of evolution. Then: why we and the trees are cousins.
questions: You share ancestors with the oak tree outside. Does that change how you feel about other living things?
Many branches of the human family went extinct. Why do you think ours survived, and was it skill or luck?
If you replayed the tape of life, do you think something like us would evolve again?

2.title: Voyage into a living cell
2.desc: Sagan pricks his finger and we dive into a white blood cell, through a nuclear pore, to watch DNA unzip and copy itself, proofreading enzyme and all.
questions: Each cell contains machinery as complex as a galaxy has stars. Why do you think the very small gets less wonder than the very large?
Mutations are mostly harmful yet drive all of evolution. Where else do mistakes turn out to be essential?
Sagan calls designing new kinds of humans "a disquieting and awesome prospect." Where would you draw the line?

2.title: Making life's building blocks, and the floaters of Jupiter
2.desc: Sparking primordial gases in a Cornell lab produces the stuff of life. Then Sagan imagines city-sized living balloons, sinkers and hunters drifting in a Jupiter-like sky.
questions: Lightning plus simple gases makes the building blocks of life in a flask. Does that make life feel more ordinary or more remarkable?
Floaters, sinkers and hunters are speculation grounded in physics. What makes a speculation responsible rather than just fantasy?
Why would finding even a single alien microbe change biology so much?

3.title: Astrology on trial
3.desc: Two newspapers, same day, contradictory horoscopes. Twins with opposite fates. And the obstetrician who had more gravitational pull on baby Carl than Mars did.
questions: Why do you think astrology survives when it fails every test? What need does it meet?
Sagan says the desire to be connected to the cosmos is real, just misdirected. In what true ways are you connected to it?
Is there a belief you hold mostly because it's comforting? How would you test it?

3.title: Pictures in the stars and the sun temples of the Anasazi
3.desc: The Big Dipper as a plow, a casserole, a bureaucrat and a hippo with a crocodile on its back. Then ancient solstice markers that catch the sun on one day a year.
questions: Every culture saw different pictures in the same stars. What does that say about how we see patterns in general?
If we named constellations today, what would we put up there, and what would that say about us?
The Anasazi could predict seasons but not a changing climate. What are we good at predicting, and what are we missing?

3.title: Wandering planets: Ptolemy, Copernicus, and young Kepler
3.desc: Why planets loop backward in the sky, the Earth-centered vs Sun-centered fight, and a lonely seminary boy who wanted to read the mind of God through geometry and the perfect solids.
questions: The Earth-centered model worked well enough to last 1,500 years. Why is "it works" not the same as "it's true"?
Copernicus was mocked as an upstart. What idea today might look foolish now but be vindicated later?
Young Kepler wanted to read the mind of God through geometry. Is the search for beauty in nature a help or a trap for science?

3.title: Kepler, Tycho Brahe, and the eight minutes of arc
3.desc: Exile, a gold-nosed Danish nobleman hoarding the best data on Earth, and the moment Kepler chooses an inconvenient eight-minute discrepancy over his beloved theory. Out come the laws of planetary motion.
questions: Kepler threw away years of work over eight minutes of arc. When have you had to let go of something you wanted to be true?
Tycho had the data and Kepler had the theory, and distrust nearly wasted both. Where do you see that problem today?
Would you have accepted the ellipse, or kept patching circles? Be honest.

3.title: War, witchcraft, and the harmony of the worlds
3.desc: The Thirty Years' War, Kepler's mother tried as a witch, the first science fiction story, and why preferring hard truth to dear illusions is the heart of science.
questions: Kepler did his best work in the middle of war, plague and his mother's witch trial. What does that say about where discovery comes from?
"He preferred the hard truth to his dearest illusions." What's one illusion you'd find hardest to give up?
Kepler's dream of space travel helped get his mother accused of witchcraft. How do new ideas get punished in your world?

4.title: Tunguska, and comets as omens of doom
4.desc: In 1908 something flattened 2,000 square km of Siberian forest and left no crater. Sagan works the mystery, then tours centuries of comet panic, including 1910's comet pills.
questions: Sagan rules out antimatter, black holes and alien ships for Tunguska. How did he decide which explanation fit best?
A comet impact could look like a nuclear attack. How should we guard against misreading a natural event in a crisis?
People bought comet pills in 1910. What's today's version of comet pills?

4.title: Comets, craters, and the monks who saw the Moon explode
4.desc: How comets get captured and crash into worlds, and five Canterbury monks in 1178 who saw fire on the Moon, an account that laser-ranging and a young crater may confirm.
questions: The Canterbury monks recorded something strange even though it went against what everyone believed. Would you have written it down?
An 800-year-old eyewitness account and a laser bounced off the Moon support each other. What makes evidence from very different sources so convincing?
Earth's craters get erased, but the Moon's don't. What other histories get erased just because of where they happened?

4.title: Velikovsky's Venus, and reading a planet from its light
4.desc: "Observation: you couldn't see a thing. Conclusion: dinosaurs." Sagan takes apart wild ideas about Venus and shows how a prism lets us read what distant worlds are made of.
questions: Sagan argues the real scandal wasn't Velikovsky being wrong, but scientists trying to suppress him. Do you agree?
"Observation: you couldn't see a thing. Conclusion: dinosaurs." Where have you seen reasoning like that?
We can tell what a star is made of from its light alone. What does that make you feel about what's knowable?

4.title: Into the hell of Venus, and a warning for Earth
4.desc: Descend with the Soviet Venera landers into sulfuric acid clouds and 900°F crushing heat: a runaway greenhouse. Then erosion, the Sphinx, and what we are doing to our own climate.
questions: Venus is a planet much like Earth that went wrong. What does it take for people to treat a warning like that seriously?
Sagan asks what account we'd give a visitor of our stewardship of Earth. What would yours be?
Slow erosion and sudden catastrophe both shape the world. Which kind of change are people worse at noticing?

5.title: War of the Worlds and Lowell's canals
5.desc: H.G. Wells' Martians, Orson Welles' panic, and Percival Lowell's Arizona observatory where he saw a dying civilization's irrigation canals that weren't there.
questions: Lowell saw canals because he expected to see them. When has expectation shaped what you saw?
Why do you think the idea of Martians gripped people so hard for a century?
Lowell was wrong but inspired a generation. Can a wrong idea still do good?

5.title: Goddard's cherry-tree dream, and the real Mars
5.desc: A boy in a cherry tree resolves to reach Mars and invents the liquid-fuel rocket. Then a flight over the real Mars: no canals, but giant volcanoes, river valleys and Valles Marineris.
questions: A kid in a cherry tree decided to reach Mars, and it shaped his whole life. Have you had a moment like that?
From orbit, even Earth's cities look lifeless at low resolution. What does that say about how we search for life?
Goddard sifted every failed rocket for clues. How do you treat your own failures?

5.title: Viking lands on Mars and looks for life
5.desc: Choosing a landing site, the first pictures from the Martian surface, and the life-detection experiments that came back tantalizing, provocative and deeply ambiguous.
questions: Viking's life experiments were "tantalizing and deeply ambiguous." How do you live with a question that has no clear answer?
Why does Sagan keep reminding us of Lowell during the Viking results?
If we did find life on Mars, how would you want the news to be handled?

5.title: What life is made of, and a rover with laser eyes
5.desc: Sagan stirs a vat of the chemicals that make a human and gets a boring mixture of atoms: the magic is in the arrangement. Plus why Mars needs a roving explorer.
questions: The chemicals in a human are worth a few dollars, but the arrangement is priceless. What does that say about what makes something valuable?
Sagan is skeptical of silicon-based life. Is it more exciting to you that life elsewhere might be like us, or totally different?
What would you want a Mars rover to go look at first?

5.title: Wolf Vishniac, and the Martians will be us
5.desc: A microbiologist who died searching for life in Antarctica's dry valleys. Then: should we terraform Mars? If we do, the Martians will be us.
questions: If Mars has life, Sagan says we should leave it alone. Do you agree, even if Mars could become a home for us?
"The Martians will be us." How do you feel about humans becoming a multi-planet species?
Is it right to spend on Mars while there are unmet needs on Earth? Where do you land on that?

6.title: Voyager sets out
6.desc: A visit to Voyager mission control as the spacecraft reaches Jupiter, and the golden record it carries for anyone who might find it among the stars.
questions: Voyager cost about a penny per world for every person on Earth. What is that kind of exploration worth?
If you had to pick one thing to put on the golden record, what would it be?
What do you think the Voyager record says about who we are, or wish we were?

6.title: The Dutch Republic: ships, maps and free minds
6.desc: 17th-century Holland as a spacefaring civilization of its day: voyages to the Spice Islands, secret charts, tolerance of heretics, and a refuge for free thinkers.
questions: The Dutch Republic thrived on trade and on tolerance. Why do you think free thought and exploration tend to go together?
Holland was a refuge for people censored elsewhere. Where are those refuges today?
The Dutch worried that greed threatened their soul. Is that worry still relevant?

6.title: Christiaan Huygens imagines other worlds
6.desc: Microscopes reveal the microbial world, telescopes reveal Titan, and Huygens dares to imagine the inhabitants of other planets and their many suns.
questions: Huygens imagined aliens much like 17th-century Europeans. What assumptions about aliens do we make that will look quaint later?
The microscope and telescope opened two hidden worlds at once. Which would you rather have discovered?
Huygens was brilliant at many things. Is being a generalist still possible, or valuable, today?

6.title: Voyager at Jupiter: Europa's cracks and Io's volcanoes
6.desc: Traveler's tales from the outer solar system: scientists arguing over Europa's strange surface in real time, and the discovery of the first active volcanoes beyond Earth.
questions: Watching scientists argue over Europa in real time, what surprises you about how science actually gets done?
Io's volcanoes weren't predicted by most people. What's the value of exploring without knowing what you'll find?
Sagan compares Voyager's discoveries to sailors' travelers' tales. What's the difference between a tale and data?

6.title: Through Saturn's rings to Titan
6.desc: Voyager's logbook, then a flight between the snowball moonlets of Saturn's rings and down toward Titan, where the building blocks of life may rain from the sky.
questions: Saturn's rings are billions of tiny moons. Does knowing what something is made of make it more or less beautiful?
Titan may rain the building blocks of life. If it does, what would that tell us about how common life is?
We stayed home and sent robots. Is that exploration, or something less?

7.title: A Brooklyn boy asks what the stars are
7.desc: Sagan walks his childhood neighborhood, remembers the library book that told him stars are suns, then visits a Brooklyn classroom to talk planets and Ganymede with kids.
questions: Sagan's curiosity was sparked by a library book. What first made you curious about the universe?
"Every one of us begins life with an open mind." What do you think closes it, and how do you keep it open?
If you could tell your eight-year-old self one fact about the cosmos, what would it be?

7.title: Campfires, myths, and the backbone of night
7.desc: How early humans explained the lights overhead: campfires of other tribes, the Milky Way as the sky's spine, Hera's spilled milk, and the capricious gods.
questions: Early humans explained the sky with what they knew: campfires, animals, gods. How do we still explain the unknown with the familiar?
Why do you think nearly every culture imagined the gods as unpredictable?
What's a myth you grew up with that you later found a natural explanation for?

7.title: The Ionian awakening: the universe is knowable
7.desc: Why science was born on the islands of the eastern Mediterranean: merchants, engineers, and Thales, who explained the world without gods, plus the Tunnel of Eupalinos.
questions: Science began at a crossroads of cultures. Why might mixing traditions make people ask better questions?
The Ionians decided the universe was knowable because it was ordered. Do you believe the universe is fully knowable?
Once you question one ritual, you start questioning others. Has that happened to you?

7.title: Empedocles' water thief and Democritus' atoms
7.desc: A kitchen gadget proves air is something real. Then Democritus cuts an apple and reasons his way to atoms and empty space, 2,400 years early.
questions: A kitchen gadget hinted at air being a real substance. What everyday object might be hiding a deep truth?
Democritus reasoned his way to atoms with no instruments at all. How far can pure reasoning take you before you need experiment?
For Democritus, understanding and enjoyment were nearly the same. Is that true for you?

7.title: Pythagoras, Plato, and the dangerous dodecahedron
7.desc: Mathematical harmony, five perfect solids, a secret too dangerous for the public, and how the Pythagoreans and Plato steered science away from experiment for 2,000 years.
questions: The Pythagoreans hid the square root of two because it broke their worldview. What uncomfortable facts get hidden today?
Sagan blames Plato and Aristotle for 2,000 years of distrust of experiment. Is that fair?
Should knowledge ever be kept from the public? Under what conditions, if any?

7.title: Aristarchus, the distance to the stars, and other planets
7.desc: The man who put the Sun at the center centuries before Copernicus, how to gauge the distance to Sirius with a brass plate, and a classroom demo of how to find hidden planets.
questions: Aristarchus was right and was ignored for 1,800 years. Why do correct ideas sometimes lose?
"We make our world significant by the courage of our questions." What's a question you've been afraid to ask?
Living in an unremarkable place in a vast universe: does that bother you or free you?

8.title: Constellations through time
8.desc: Every constellation is one frame in a cosmic movie. Sagan runs the sky forward and back a million years, watching the Big Dipper and Orion fall apart.
questions: Constellations look permanent only because our lives are short. What else looks permanent to you only because of your timescale?
When you look at old starlight, you're seeing the past. How does it feel that the sky is a history book?
Would you rather travel through space or through time, and why?

8.title: Einstein on a bicycle in Tuscany: riding a light beam
8.desc: A teenage Einstein wonders what you'd see riding a light wave. Then a scooter ride near light speed: the world squeezes, colors shift, and a twin comes home younger than his brother.
questions: Einstein got there by questioning something everyone took for granted. What assumption in your life might be worth questioning?
A twin comes home younger than his brother. Which part of relativity feels most impossible to you, and why accept it anyway?
Relativity sets limits on what we can do. How do you feel about the universe having rules that don't bend to our ambitions?

8.title: Leonardo's flying machines, starships, and time travel
8.desc: Leonardo was trapped in his century. Could we be too? Nuclear-pulse starships Orion and Daedalus, a 1g ride across the galaxy, and what we'd change if we could travel to the past.
questions: Leonardo was trapped in an age that couldn't build his ideas. What ideas of ours might be waiting on a future age?
A starship trip could leave everyone you know long dead when you return. Would you go?
If you could change one moment in history, would you, knowing it might erase the present?

8.title: Worlds forming, and the branch points of history
8.desc: Watch a solar system condense from dust, imagine the planets of other stars, then rewind evolution: if history had been a little different, who would be here instead of us?
questions: If evolution replayed slightly differently, someone else would be here. Does that make our existence feel fragile or lucky?
Sagan says we're at a branch point in history. What branch point do you think we're at right now?
Our solar system may be just one type among many. Does variety in the universe excite or unsettle you?

9.title: To make an apple pie, first invent the universe
9.desc: The famous line, then Sagan keeps cutting a slice of pie in half until he reaches atoms. Mirrors, infinity, the googol and the googolplex.
questions: "To make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe." What everyday thing in your life has a cosmic backstory?
A googolplex can't even be written out in our universe. How do you think about numbers too big to imagine?
How far down can you keep cutting something before it stops being that thing? What does that say about identity?

9.title: Atoms, elements, and why the stars shine
9.desc: The 92 natural elements, how protons and neutrons build each one, and the fusion of hydrogen into helium that lights every star, including a tour of our turbulent Sun.
questions: Everything you've ever seen is made of about 92 kinds of atoms. Is that simplicity beautiful or reductive?
Stars shine by turning hydrogen into helium. How does it feel that sunlight is the result of nuclear fusion?
Alchemists dreamed of making gold. Physics can, but it isn't worth it. What dreams come true in ways we didn't expect?

9.title: How stars die, and the supernova the Anasazi saw
9.desc: Red giants, the Sun's distant death, supernovas forging the heavy elements, cosmic rays clicking in a Geiger counter in a cave, and a pictograph of the explosion of 1054.
questions: The Sun will one day swallow Earth. Does knowing the far future change how you think about the present?
The Anasazi may have painted a supernova a thousand years ago. What would you record for the future if you saw something unprecedented?
Cosmic rays from distant explosions may have caused mutations in your ancestors. How connected do you feel to events that far away?

9.title: Neutron stars, black holes, and a gravity tea party
9.desc: A spoonful of neutron star would punch through the Earth. Sagan plays with gravity until tea floats, light bends back on itself, and a black hole might lead to elsewhere and elsewhen.
questions: A black hole might lead somewhere else entirely. How do you weigh beautiful speculation against what we can test?
Gravity can be so strong that light can't escape. What other forces have an absolute point of no return?
Which feels stranger to you: neutron stars, black holes, or curved space? Why?

9.title: We are made of star stuff
9.desc: Why the stars aren't remote from us at all: the atoms in us were forged in them. And the dawn you'd see from a planet inside a globular cluster.
questions: The atoms in your body were forged in stars. Does that change how you see yourself?
From a planet in a globular cluster, dawn would be thousands of suns rising. What's the most beautiful sky you've ever seen?
Sagan says our matter and form are set by the cosmos. Where does that leave free will?

10.title: The birth of the universe and colliding galaxies
10.desc: From the Big Bang to the first galaxies, then billions of years compressed into seconds as galaxies spin, collide and spill their stars into the void.
questions: Most cultures understand their own birth through myth. How does the Big Bang compare as a creation story?
Galaxies collide over hundreds of millions of years. What does it take to think on timescales that long?
Quasars were a mystery when this aired. How comfortable are you with science saying "we don't know yet"?

10.title: Doppler shifts and the janitor who found the expanding universe
10.desc: A passing train's whistle explains red shift. Milton Humason, a mule driver turned Mount Wilson janitor, and Hubble discover the galaxies are rushing away.
questions: Humason went from mule driver to janitor to discovering the expanding universe. What does that say about who gets to do science?
A train whistle helped reveal the universe's history. What ordinary experience might explain something huge?
The galaxies are all moving away from us, yet we're not at the center. How does that work, and how does it make you feel?

10.title: Flatland and the fourth dimension
10.desc: Sagan's legendary explanation: a flat creature visited by a 3D apple, a cube's shadow, the tesseract, and how our universe might be curved through a dimension we can't see.
questions: To a Flatlander, a 3D visitor appears from nowhere. What might we be missing because we can't perceive it?
We can't picture a fourth dimension but we can reason about it. How much should we trust ideas we can't visualize?
If our universe were curved, you could travel in a straight line and come home. What feels most mind-bending about that?

10.title: The Hindu cosmos and the oscillating universe
10.desc: The only ancient religion whose timescales match modern cosmology: a day and night of Brahma, 8.64 billion years. Shiva's dance and an endlessly reborn universe.
questions: Hindu cosmology's timescales roughly match modern science, by accident. Why do you think that resonates with people?
"If God always existed, why not save a step and say the universe always existed?" How do you respond?
Would you prefer a universe that ends once, or one that cycles forever? Why?

10.title: Listening with radio telescopes at the edge of forever
10.desc: The Very Large Array and a universe revealed in radio and X-ray light, plus how mapping galaxies by the million showed a universe of bubbles.
questions: Radio telescopes work with energies smaller than a snowflake hitting the ground. What does that say about patience in science?
Most of the universe is invisible to our eyes. How does knowing that change what "seeing" means?
We're poised "at the edge of forever." What question about the universe do you most want answered in your lifetime?

11.title: A water world, and the songs of whales
11.desc: The aliens of Earth's oceans, then the great whales: 15-minute songs with the information of an epic poem, once heard across whole oceans until our ships drowned them out.
questions: Whale songs may hold as much information as an epic poem. Do you think whales have something like culture?
Our ships drowned out a conversation that had gone on for millions of years. What else might we be drowning out without noticing?
Why might it be easier for us to imagine aliens in space than to recognize intelligence in our own oceans?

11.title: The library in every cell, and the library in your head
11.desc: Each cell carries a thousand volumes of genetic instructions. Then the brain: reptile core, mammal emotions, a cortex holding 20 million books' worth, and one of Sagan's earliest memories.
questions: Your genes hold a thousand volumes, your brain far more. Which matters more to who you are: what you inherited or what you learned?
The reptile brain handles aggression and ritual. Where do you see it running the show, in yourself or in society?
Sagan can still recall one of his earliest memories. What's yours, and why do you think it stuck?

11.title: The city as brain, and what an astonishing thing a book is
11.desc: New York grows like a brain, keeping its old parts. Then Sagan's ode to books: a flat object made from a tree, through which an author speaks across millennia.
questions: Cities and brains both keep their old parts while adding new ones. What "old wiring" in your thinking still shapes you?
"What an astonishing thing a book is." Which book has spoken to you most clearly across time?
Books let us talk to the dead. What do you want to leave behind that someone could read in a thousand years?

11.title: A global brain, and the Voyager record
11.desc: Ideas as the genes of culture, what alien brains might be like, and the golden record: a message in a bottle cast into the cosmic ocean.
questions: Ideas reproduce and get selected like genes. Which ideas do you think are spreading fastest today, and are they the good ones?
The Voyager record is a message in a bottle. If you could add one sentence to it, what would it say?
Sagan imagined a global intelligence linking all brains on Earth. Did the internet become that? Is it a good one?

12.title: UFOs and the Betty and Barney Hill abduction
12.desc: Why haven't aliens visited? Sagan examines the most famous abduction story and its star map, and gives us "extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence."
questions: "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence." What's an extraordinary claim you've believed without that evidence?
Why are personal stories so persuasive even when they're weak evidence?
If aliens did visit, what kind of evidence would actually convince you?

12.title: Champollion cracks the hieroglyphics
12.desc: A boy sees hieroglyphs nobody can read and vows to decipher them. Decades later he walks into the temples of Egypt and reads walls that waited half a million nights for a reader.
questions: Champollion's childhood question became his life's work. What question would you devote years to answering?
Others assumed hieroglyphs were mystical symbols; Champollion treated them as language. How does the right assumption unlock a problem?
Decoding Egypt is practice for decoding aliens. What would be hardest about understanding a truly alien mind?

12.title: How to talk to aliens, and the Drake equation
12.desc: Science as the universal language, the Arecibo radio dish, then Sagan works through the famous equation for how many civilizations might be out there.
questions: Sagan argues science and math are a universal language. Is there anything else every intelligent species would share?
In the Drake equation, the biggest unknown is how long civilizations last. What do you think decides that?
Are you optimistic or pessimistic about how many civilizations are out there? What drives your guess?

12.title: The Encyclopaedia Galactica
12.desc: What a first message might look like, why they might not have come, and leafing through a galactic encyclopedia of worlds, all the way to the entry for Earth.
questions: If there are so many civilizations, why no contact? Which answer to that puzzle do you find most convincing?
Searching for alien signals costs less than a weapons overrun. What does that say about our priorities?
If the Encyclopaedia Galactica had an entry for Earth today, what would it say?

13.title: The Tlingit meet La Pérouse, and a dream of a dead world
13.desc: "Choose life." A peaceful 1786 first contact in Alaska, then Sagan dreams of returning to Earth and finding it silent. What would the galactic encyclopedia say about us?
questions: The Tlingit and La Pérouse chose peace; the conquistadors chose plunder. What decides which way a first contact goes?
Sagan dreams of returning to a silent Earth. What would you most regret us losing?
"Choose life." What does that mean on the scale of a civilization, and on the scale of one person?

13.title: A blockbuster for every family
13.desc: The reptile brain and the bomb: how the world built more than 10,000 megatons of nuclear weapons, what they would do, and how humanity has outgrown old evils before.
questions: Everyone calls the arms race madness, and every country has an excuse. How do intelligent people end up trapped in collective madness?
Slavery was with us for thousands of years and was mostly ended. What gives you hope that other old evils can end too?
Which part of human nature do you think will win out: the old reptile brain or the newer cortex?

13.title: Hypatia and the end of the Library
13.desc: Back to Alexandria: why the city never shared its discoveries, the murder of Hypatia, and the burning of the last of the library. What we lost, and why it could happen again.
questions: The Library's discoveries were never shared with ordinary people, so no one defended it. What knowledge today is in that position?
Hypatia was killed partly for what she symbolized. Why are symbols of learning sometimes targets?
What's one thing you could do to make science more accessible to someone in your life?

13.title: A story about the beginning
13.desc: Fifteen billion years told as one story, from fusion in the first stars to molecules that copy themselves to us, then a montage of humanity and the wonder of discovery.
questions: Fifteen billion years told as one story sounds like myth, but it's evidence-based. Does that story move you the way myths do?
An alien would find our cultural differences trivial compared to what we share. Do you agree?
Where were you the first time you felt real wonder about the universe?

13.title: Who speaks for Earth? It's up to you
13.desc: Science as the best tool we have, the first footprints on the Moon, and Sagan's closing words: our loyalties are to the species and the planet. We speak for Earth.
questions: "Our loyalties are to the species and the planet." How would the world change if most people really felt that?
Sagan calls science "the best tool we have," but not perfect. Where is it misused, and how do we guard against that?
After the whole series, what's the one idea from Cosmos you most want to carry with you?
Who speaks for Earth? Do you?
